@bruvzg @Rindbee PTAL

Hello, Godot team and contributors! I have a question for everyone:

Currently, .NET is not officially compatible with the OpenHarmony system. I forked the dotnet/runtime repository and adapted the NativeAOT runtime for the OpenHarmony system(https://github.com/OpenHarmony-NET/runtime).



Due to issues like non-standard build scripts, I haven't submitted a pull request to the dotnet/runtime repository. I've only compiled the static library files for the NativeAOT runtime and uploaded them to GitHub https://github.com/OpenHarmony-NET/OpenHarmony.NET.Runtime.

If .NET developers want to develop dynamic libraries for HarmonyOS, they need to clone the repository locally, reference the target files in their csproj files, and use the linux-musl-architecture rid for nativeaot publishing.

If the .NET adaptation for HarmonyOS is never merged into the official repository, and Godot supports .NET on the HarmonyOS platform, how OpenHarmony's .NET be distributed it will be accepted by Godot??

> Is there a simulator of OpenHarmony? I was able to build a template and export it on macOS, but not sure how to test it without the device.

The IDE developed by Huawei for OpenHarmony includes an OpenHarmony emulator, but it is based on the x64 architecture, while almost all OpenHarmony or HarmonyOS devices on sale are based on the arm64 architecture.

dowload url: https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/cn/deveco-studio/

Additionally, the simulator imposes looser restrictions on applications than on a real device. For example:
1. Some syscalls are prohibited on a real device, causing crashes, while the simulator won't (they might be allowed or return an error code; I haven't noticed, but they definitely won't crash).
2. JIT is not allowed on a real device, meaning requests for executable memory are prohibited, while the simulator has no restrictions.
3. The compatibility of GPU is slightly different. When I adapted Avalonia, I found that PC does not support ARGB format textures, while the real machine does.
4. There may be more.

> If .NET developers want to develop dynamic libraries for HarmonyOS, they need to clone the repository locally, reference the target files in their csproj files, and use the linux-musl-architecture rid for nativeaot publishing. > > If the .NET adaptation for HarmonyOS is never merged into the official repository, and Godot supports .NET on the HarmonyOS platform, how OpenHarmony's .NET be distributed it will be accepted by Godot?? AFAIK, Godot itself doesn't care how developers compile C# projects. Therefore, whether the .NET community officially supports OpenHarmony or uses the community-driven OpenHarmony.Net has no impact on Godot's implementation. In addition, this PR does not include C# scripting support. You can see how I implemented C# scripting support in Godot in this [branch](https://github.com/kdada/godot/commits/openharmony/): Current rid is: https://github.com/kdada/godot/commit/c237b021c9ce349e63edd3263fb41faef49976b9#diff-8eea20745c13343ba72e1a19718f4869d2c547661bbde53538ce15d7408c9767R231 ``` if (platform == OS.Platforms.OpenHarmony) { runtimeIdentifier = $"linux-musl-{ridArch}"; } ```

> As far as the export process is concerned, there is no problem exporting unsigned apps, but there will be an error when exporting signed apps (probably an issue with hvigorw). > > Additionally, the requirements for directly exporting a signed app are a bit demanding and not well documented. Here are my summary of the requirements (I'm using Command Line Tools version 5.1.0, maybe I should try an earlier version, which can be found on the [Chinese page](https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/cn/download/command-line-tools-for-hmos)): > > - It requires that the length of storePassword and keyPassword must be an even number not less than 32; > - It requires that there must be a directory named material in the directory where the .p12 file is located; > - The material directory should contain subdirectories named ac, ce, and fd. I'm not sure how to generate these files manually, so directly exporting the signed app fails. @Rindbee For information on how to generate the files required for signing, please refer to the docs:: - Store File (*.p12): https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/en/doc/harmonyos-guides/ide-signing#section297715173233 - Following this doc, you will create p12 and the corresponding material/{ac,ce,fd} directories - Cert Path File (*.cer): https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/en/doc/app/agc-help-add-releasecert-0000001946273961 - Profile File (*.p7b): https://developer.huawei.com/consumer/en/doc/app/agc-help-add-releaseprofile-0000001914714796 To set the Store Password and Key Password, first add the above files to the IDE and enter the passwords. The IDE will then generate an encrypted Store Password and Key Password in build-profile.json5. Add the encrypted Store Password and Key Password to the Godot export configuration to enable automatic signing: The IDE doesn't expose how to encrypt the Store Password and Key Password, so currently, it's not possible to sign apps using raw passwords. However, as you suggested, using `hap-sign-tool.jar` is a good option. I'll improve the signing process to use `hap-sign-tool.jar`.

> Is this just being left to gather dust?

The Godot maintainers have not made their stance on supporting OpenHarmony clear. As a result, this PR remains based on Godot 4.4.1 and has not been updated to keep up with the main branch.

After reporting bugs to two OpenHarmony repositories ([openharmony/docs#106125](https://gitcode.com/openharmony/docs/issues/106125) and [openharmony/interface_sdk_c#4261](https://gitcode.com/openharmony/interface_sdk_c/issues/4261)) twenty days ago with no results, I’ve lost interest in following OpenHarmony.

Browsing the issues in these two repositories makes me doubt my Chinese comprehension skills.
